Figure 52 compares the road type distribution in FleetDNA, CE-CERT, and their combination to MOVES3. Table 3 gives the conversion from numeric road type to description: 2 is rural freeway, 3 is rural other road, 4 is urban freeway, and 5 is urban other road. In contrast to other source types, for combination-unit long-haul vehicles, we see the highest concentration of miles driven on rural freeways, with rural other roads in second place. Because FleetDNA contains 70 combination-unit long-haul vehicles and nearly 18,000 driving hours logged, we would recommend shifting the MOVES distribution to match FleetDNA by increasing the VMT on rural freeways and decreasing it on urban roads, as seen in the top left chart of Figure 52. The large amount of driving on rural freeways (~50%) is also intuitively characteristic of the behavior of these vehicles. For the rest of the source types, we see that the FleetDNA and CE- CERT data tend to track vehicles in urban roads much more, and rural VMT is almost negligible. The road type distributions in MOVES3 are based on national values from data used to derive the 2017 National Emissions Inventory (EPA 2021). Because the road type distribution for individual fleets should vary substantially whether the fleet is in an urban or rural area, and the data we have collected for other source types than combination-unit long-haul are from urban fleets, we do not recommend that the proportion between urban and rural be used to update the national defaults. However, within the urban fleets, the ratio of freeway to other roads are useful to compare to MOVES and may be suggestive of improvements to current data. The FleetDNA data suggest relatively more driving occurs on urban other roads compared to urban freeways for all vehicles except for combination long-haul trucks. CE-CERT tends to show more time on urban freeways than urban other roads—with the exception of airport shuttle “other” buses.
